pages.text: A lantern swings up the road in the daylight. Under it walks Pieter, the night watchman. He does not look happy.
“I am sorry, {player}. The Lord wants his share. It is not my idea. I only carry the book.” He shows you a number. “Pay when you can. I will wait at the gate.”

c3_pieter_paid.title: Pieter
c3_pieter_paid.text: Pieter taps his book shut. “Thank you. Most people hide when they see me.” He almost smiles. Then he walks home, whistling a tune he does not know he is whistling.

c3_k_pieter.text: Far down the road, a lantern waves at you. Pieter. You wave back.

c3_letter.title: Stay if you must
c3_letter.text: Another letter comes from the river barge. Your mother writes: “Stay if you must. Your cousin asks after you.” You read the last line again. To you it sounds like a warning.

c3_miller.title: The miller on the bridge
c3_miller.text: On the bridge, the miller glares down at the stream. It is still very low. He glares at you, too, just in case.

c3_forge.title: Clang
c3_forge.text: Old Odinson lights the forge and young Bo works the bellows. They show you how to hold the tongs. “Good hands,” says Odinson, which is the most he has said all day. Bo grins at the fire.

pages.text: In the old mill, on a rusty nail, hangs a bell. It is far too small for a cow. It is far too small for anything. It sways, just a little, though there is no wind.
In the dust beneath it you think you see tiny footprints. You look the other way. You are quite sure that you looked the other way.

c3_stream.title: The stream runs again
c3_stream.text: The stream runs clear again. On the bridge the miller looks down at the water. Then at you. He nods once, a very small nod. That is his whole apology, and you take it.

c3_dance.title: The harvest dance
c3_dance.text: You work the cider while the village dances. Mugs float above the heads. One falls, you catch it, and you laugh out loud. Somewhere close by, something goes tink, like a very small bell. You do not look.

pages.text: A goat trots up the path and straight into the brambles nobody could clear. Crunch. Munch. She eats thistles as if they were sweets. You open your mouth to stop her. Then you let her.
The third line of the old rhyme comes back, and you say it with your mouth still open: “Brave goat clears the bramble bed.” The goat looks at your hat. Her eyes are thoughtful.

c3_goat_out.title: A scarecrow in your hat
c3_goat_out.text: In the morning the scarecrow is wearing your hat. Nobody saw who put it there. Under the hat there is a letter: “Your cousin may come to visit.” You take your hat back. It is still warm.

c3_frame3.title: Back in the room
c3_frame3.text: “Were you scared of the cousin?” asks somebody from under a blanket. “More than of any imp,” you say. “What's an imp?” “Shh!” say three children at once. “That comes later!”
